en: Although Zen takes the non-reliance on words and letters and the non-dependence on cultivation or realization as its primary principle, since there is something to be investigated, there must necessarily be a "key" (yào).
What is this key? It is like the main rope of a net or the collar of a garment; it is that which allows a person to grasp it once and directly attain the straight path.
It is not that the myriad meshes do not constitute a net, but if one discards the main rope and attempts to lift the meshes, the net will certainly not hold.
Zhang said: "Ten thousand threads are not what do not constitute clothing; yet if one pulls at the collar and lifts the threads, the garment will surely be disarrayed.
Yongjia said: "I am not one who plucks leaves or seeks branches; for branches and leaves are not the essentials—the root is truly essential.

Students, moreover, are often ignorant of this root. Guoshan said: "The essential point lies in the person's ability to choose; one may choose the superior and follow the good. Thus it is with students.
Often, one makes a mistaken decision at the very start, resulting in traveling northward when intending to reach Yue.

Even though the collected writings of the ancestral masters from antiquity are as vast as mountains, and every single word and phrase is undoubtedly a fundamental principle, alas, as the ages have passed and the sages are distant, falsehoods and deceptions have daily increased. When the mind, intellect, and consciousness are corrupted by them, those who regard these fundamental principles as mere trivial details— [The text continues:

...are indeed [those who... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a classical Chinese commentary on Zen or Buddhist doctrine. The translation reflects the philosophical and literary style of the original.)
Alas! My teacher, Master Gaofeng,
for over twenty years since moving from Shuangfeng to Xifeng, has out of necessity pointed directly at the core for others—
like a divine medicine of a few grains that raises the dead, or a numinous talisman with a single stroke that drives away demons.
This is false. Therefore, there are those who seek out its extraordinary methods and secret mantras, intending to take them as the guiding principles for their disciples.

Some may say: "In catching birds, it is the eyes that matter, not the net; in warding off the cold, it is the threads that matter, not the collar. Of the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, every gate can be entered.
Thus, the eyes and the threads are truly not essential. To this, one should respond: "The Dharma-gates of the World-Honored One are indeed vast."
The Great is boundless. Yet, you have provisionally established a single, narrow gate as a skillful means (*upāya*), causing all sons to emerge from the burning house and enter the Mahāyāna;
this is merely taking the mesh of the net and making it the mainstay of the collar. Now, is it the mainstay or the mesh?
Is it the collar or the threads? Is it essential or non-essential? Without possessing the correct eye on the crown of the head, one cannot speak lightly of this—your venerable ancestor.

Since joining the dharma assembly at Xifeng, I have periodically transcribed and compiled those dharma discourses shown to my disciples that were most urgent for resolving matters of practice, naming them "Essentials of Chan" (Canyao).
I have long desired to share these with those who possess the aspiration [for the Way].

One day, I presented them to the Venerable Yongzhong of Gusu, who joyfully wished to solicit donations to carve them into woodblocks and requested that I, Qiaozu, write a preface. Having done so, Qiaozu—[the text continues].
Having received his command, he further told him: "The Master has another essential teaching that lies outside the formal framework.
It is hidden within the skeletal voids of space; neither you, elder brother, nor I can carve it into print or provide a preface. We must wait for another day to reveal it once more."
Written on the Double Ninth day of the Jiawu year of the Zhizhen era by Hong Qiaozu, Zhigong, a student at Tianmu.
Guling regarded the study of scriptures as nothing more than boring through old paper; Lun Pian regarded reading books as merely tasting dregs.

This is because the Way cannot be sought through speech or written characters. Yet, the Way has no fixed location or substance, and no form or likeness; it is not something that can be expressed by words.

Regarding words and written characters: by what means can they be clarified? Therefore, although our Buddha, the World-Honored One, transformed and guided beings according to their capacities, skillfully accomplishing his subtle and profound work, he could not help but discourse upon the twelve divisions of the Dharma.

When Bodhidharma came from the West, although he did not establish reliance on written characters, at the moment of transmission, he passed down the teachings through oral tradition and face-to-face instruction; thus, he too could not dispense with speech. For although the Way—
It does not reside within words and letters, yet it is truly not separate from words and letters.

The subtle and profound essence is contained within the surface of verbal expression, making it difficult to perceive. Scholars of the world often sink into the literal meaning of the words and fail to grasp its subtle essence;
they merely follow the finger pointing at the moon, never beholding the moon itself in the sky.
Consequently, they took speech and written characters as obstacles, leading the ancient Lin Qian to exclaim in indignation that they were nothing more than "rotten paper and dregs.
Yet, speech and written characters are precisely the means by which the blossoms of the mind are revealed and the subtleties of the Way are modeled;
how could they have ever obstructed the Way?
Master Gaofeng’s preaching of the Dharma was like clouds and rain. Master Zhizhong Hongjun extracted its most extraordinary and secret essentials and titled them *Canyao* (Essentials of Chan).

The Venerable Yongzhong subsequently carved these into woodblocks to broaden their dissemination. This is like catching the main rope when casting a net or grasping the collar when pulling a fur coat;
it intends to enable students to realize the totality of the Way’s essence by means of these essential dharma-words. Its...
To open the minds of later students can truly be called earnest. If students are indeed able to seek this with leisurely ease and pursue it with joyful devotion,
so that their doubts are forever dispelled and their principles are harmoniously understood, then the sequence of their practice and the essentials of their progress will become clear.
The Master has laid everything bare; it is all contained within this book. My only concern is that students may fail to take it up with fierce resolve. Alas!
When Bian Que is at hand, he possesses efficacious medicines—some called "Divine Elixirs," others "Sorrowless Powders"—which restore life from death, their efficacy achieved in a single instant.
Those who possess the eye of wisdom, apply their spirit, and exert their full strength must pursue this with urgent diligence.
Yet those who seek it have never failed to find it.
How could the words of the Master deceive you? Students, be careful not to mistake this for the words of the ancient Lin Qian.
Yet, lest we forget the earnest instructions of our late teacher, it is my hope that Master Zhicheng Yongzhong’s efforts will not have been in vain,
and that those who study this record of his words and attain enlightenment shall not leave such glory solely to those who came before.
On the first day of the waning moon of the tenth month in the Jia-wu year of the Zhiyuan era,
the student Qingtao Jingming Zhu Yingyuan respectfully inscribed this postscript to the *Essentials of Chan* by Master Gaofeng.
Compiled by the Attendant and Record-Holder,
the Practitioner of the Way, Layman Zhigong Hong Qiaozu.
Opening the Hall for a General Discourse.
A monk asked, "The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;

with an empty mind, they return as top graduates. Master, when Layman Pang spoke thus, was there anything therein intended for the benefit of others? The Master said, "There is. The monk pressed further:
"In the end, it lies within that single phrase. The Master said, "Bring forward the question from the beginning.
The student asked, "What is the 'assembly where the ten directions gather together'? The Master said, "Dragons and snakes are intermingled; ordinary people and sages meet.

The student asked, "What is 'each and every one studying non-action'? The Master said, "Mouth swallowing Buddhas and patriarchs; eyes overshadowing heaven and earth. The student asked, "What is 'selecting the Buddha'?"

[The Master] said, "Ten thousand miles east and west, eight thousand miles south and north. The monk stepped forward and asked, "What is it like to return home having attained the highest rank with a mind empty of conceptualization?
The Master said, "A movement of the countenance reveals the ancient path; one does not fall into the trap of silent stillness.

The monk asked, "If that is so, then every word manifests the ultimate truth, and every phrase points toward the source. The Master said, "Where do you see this? The monk gave a shout. The Master said, "That too is merely tossing about [the head]."
[The Master] struck the moon with his staff. Jìn said, "Let us set this matter aside for a moment.

Just as today at Xīfēng, where the assembly from the ten directions has gathered and the Field for Selecting Buddhas is opened—what auspicious signs are there ultimately? The Master said, "Mountains, rivers, the great earth, and the myriad phenomena—all sentient and insentient beings—shall all attain Buddhahood.
Jìn said, "If all have already attained Buddhahood, for what reason do you, a student, not attain Buddhahood?"
The Master said, "If you were to become a Buddha, how could you cause the entire earth to become a Buddha?

The monk asked, "Ultimately, where does the student's fault lie? The Master said, "South of Xiang, north of Tan. The monk asked, "Do you permit the student to repent? The Master said, "Prostrate yourself.

As soon as the monk prostrated, the Master said, "A lion bites a man; a hunting dog chases after clods of earth. The Master [said]: "The lion bites a man; the hunting dog chases after clods. The Master [said].
He then raised his whisk and addressed the assembly, saying: "This is the field for selecting Buddhas; those who have attained the 'first place' through the emptiness of mind return here.
O clever ones, if you can see it within this very place, you will see where Layman Pang established his body and life.
Once you see where Layman Pang established his body and life, you will see where all the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past established their bodies and lives. Once you see the Buddhas..."
Where the Patriarch established his body and life, there one sees for oneself the place where one establishes one’s own body and life.

Having seen for oneself this place of establishing body and life, it is no hindrance to here break off the staff, hang up the alms-bowl bag, and beneath the three rafters and before the seven-foot mat, eat rice-less gruel and drink unsullied soup;
stretching out one's legs to sleep, one passes the time in carefree ease.
If you cannot distinguish between master and servant, nor differentiate beans from wheat, and if you are driven by necessity,
I shall temporarily set aside my lofty perspective and, within the void, write this "Upadhyaya" (The Great Man) for all people to follow like a painted cat.
Many years ago, when I returned to the hall at Shuangjing after a month had not yet passed, I suddenly became suspicious of the myriad dharmas while asleep.
"Where does this 'one' return? From this point, a state of doubt suddenly arose within him. He forgot to sleep and lost his appetite;

he could no longer distinguish east from west or day from night. Whether opening his bedding and spreading out his bowl, or defecating and urinating—even in every movement and stillness, every word and silence—it was all nothing but the question:
"Where does this one return? Not even a hair’s breadth of a different thought arose, nor did he wish for one to arise.
Not even the slightest thought of difference can be found; it is just like a nail driven into wood or glue adhering to a surface—shaken and moved, yet it does not budge.
Even amidst a vast multitude, he is as if no one else exists. From morning until evening, and from evening until morning, he is limpid and profound, steadfast and towering.

Pure and clear, utterly free of a single speck of defilement; a single thought lasts ten thousand years. The environment is stilled and the person is forgotten, as if in a state of innocent ignorance.
It was as if he were dazed. Unaware that it had already been the sixth day, he was following the assembly in chanting sutras at the Three Pagodas.

Suddenly, lifting his head, he beheld the portrait of the Fifth Patriarch, Master Yuan. At that moment, he was struck with sudden awakening regarding the "sentence about dragging a corpse" that the old master Yangshan had asked him about days before.
It was as if empty space were pulverized and the great earth were submerged; subject and object were both forgotten, like an image reflected in a mirror.
The Mirror; Baizhang’s Wild Fox; the Dog Has Buddha-nature; the Qingzhou Cloth Robe;
the Story of the Woman Emerging from Samādhi—these have been raised subtly from the beginning, and upon examination, none remain unclear. The wondrous function of Prajñā is truly not a falsehood.

Regarding the "Mu" (No) character I have been contemplating for nearly three years, with the exception of the two meals of porridge and rice, I have never once leaned against my meditation cushion, nor have I even leaned on it when weary.
Alas! Although day and night one moves eastward and westward, one is constantly rolled into a single mass with the two demons of dullness and distraction.
Though they exhaust every artifice, these cannot be dispelled; for this "Mu" (No), one has never once exerted even a moment’s effort.
After achieving a state of unified resolve, I have investigated the source of my ailment and found no other cause: it is simply because I have not been in a state of doubt.
In applying effort to the mind, one simply holds [the object] at all times. When held, it exists;
when not held, it is absent. Even if one wishes to give rise to doubt, there is no place to begin.

Even if one were able to apply oneself and manage to harbor doubt, in a mere instant, one cannot avoid being struck by dullness and distraction, splitting the matter into two pieces. Thus, one wastes a great deal of time and labor in vain.
For many lifetimes one has received [this teaching], yet there is not even a trace of progress; where does it all lead? This is, however, different from the "Mu" (No) koan.
Here, doubt easily arises; as soon as it is raised, it is present without waiting for repeated reflection, calculation, or deliberate mental effort.
Once the state of doubt begins to coalesce into a continuous mass, the mind loses its power to act. Since the mind no longer possesses the capacity to act, [the karmic burden]...
Thoughts are immediately forgotten. This causes the myriad conditions that do not cease to cease of their own accord; the six sense-gates that are not tranquil to become tranquil of their own accord.

Without violating even a speck of dust, one suddenly enters the *asamāhita-samādhi* (the samādhi of no-mind). When unexpectedly encountering the moment of eating gruel or rice, one will surely reach for the spoon and chopsticks by the side of the bowl.
One need not fear the turtle escaping from the jar. This is a method already proven effective; it is certain.

Do not deceive one another. If there were even a single phrase that deluded others, one would incur the karmic retribution of falling eternally into the plow-field hell where one's tongue is pulled out.
You who are currently studying Prajñāpāramitā must clearly understand this momentous matter; do not shrink from mountains high or waters wide.

I have come specifically to see you at this western peak; moreover, each of you has lit fingers and burned incense, established precepts and vows, and sharpened your will with the resolve of iron and stone.

Since you possess such character and insight, and such understanding and vision, you must by all means not betray your own original aspiration, nor betray your parents’ intention in renouncing you for the sake of leaving home, nor betray the donors who have newly constructed this Sangha hall.
Faith and confidence. Do not辜负 (betray) the protective heart of the kings, ministers, and patrons. Go directly downward with great faith; go directly downward without change or deviation;
go directly downward standing like a ten-thousand-fathom cliff; go directly downward relying on the painted cat.

Paint it again and again until you reach the place where the cross-hatched patterns meet, the place where the paths of consciousness are cut off, and the place where both person and phenomena are forgotten. The brush—
Suddenly, from beneath the tip [of the staff], a live cat leaps forth. Ha! Originally, the entire great earth is a field for selecting Buddhas;
the entire great earth is one’s own self. Reaching this point, what need is there to speak of Layman Pang?

Even if the Three Vehicles and the Ten Stages were to lose heart and their souls tremble in terror, even the blue-eyed barbarian and the yellow-headed one would have no place to set foot. Nevertheless, if...
One must open the eye of the human and celestial realms and propagate the ancestral legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs;

furthermore, one must fuse oneself with the field for selecting Buddhas into a single mass and cast it beyond hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of worlds, then turn the body and shift the step.
"Go one step further, even beyond that side of Vīranandin! Then come and receive the heavy staff from West Peak.
"O assembly, since you have already cast yourself away, what is there left for you to receive the staff?

Suddenly, if there were a man who disregarded his own life, upon hearing such a statement, he might come forth, overturn the meditation seat, and shout the assembly into dispersal—if this were so, it would indeed be so.
It is so. Yet, for now, the Lion Rock on the western peak has not yet consented to nod its head.
To the assembly:
throughout the three periods of time, all Buddhas and successive patriarchs have left behind a word or a half-phrase, solely intent upon enabling sentient beings to transcend [the mundane].
The three realms are severed from the flow of birth and death; therefore it is said that [the Buddha] appeared in the world for the sake of this one great matter.
If one discusses this one great matter, it is like two horses boxing face-to-face, or like threading a needle within a flash of lightning.
There is no place for you to deliberate or understand; there is no place for you to calculate or discriminate. Thus it is said: "This Dharma is not of thought."
This cannot be understood through the analytical capacity of the intellect.
Therefore, O World-Honored One, at the final moment on the summit of Vulture Peak, you overturned the three hundred and sixty bones and eighty-four thousand pores to their very depths.
Although a multitude of a million people surrounded you, the one who could truly take it up was none other than Kāśyapa alone. Thus we know with certainty that this matter is by no means...
Roughly stated: if you desire a true and clear realization, you must open a mind of exceptional penetration and manifest the resolve of a man of integrity.

You must cast away all your former evil knowledge and misconceptions, as well as those wondrous words and exquisite phrases—Chan, the Way, and the Buddha-dharma—all that you have seen with your eyes throughout your entire life.
Regarding whatever is heard by the ears, disregard danger and ruin, gain and loss, self and other, right and wrong, reaching or not reaching, and penetrating or not penetrating.
Give rise to great wrath and brandish the sharp edge of the vajra, as if cutting a handful of silk threads: with one cut, all are severed;
once severed, they never continue again. One must reach the state where the center of the chest is empty and vast, and void.

Vast and open, expansive and unconfined, there is not even a hair’s breadth of obstruction. Furthermore, there is not a single dharma that can engage the mind. It is no different from being newly born.
Drinking tea, one does not know the tea; eating rice, one does not know the rice; walking, one does not know walking; sitting, one does not know sitting.
Sentient consciousness is suddenly purified and all calculating deliberations are forgotten. It is exactly like a living corpse.

Furthermore, it is like a figure made of clay or carved from wood. Upon reaching this point, suddenly tripping or stumbling, the flower of the mind blossoms all at once, illuminating the ten directions as clearly as the bright sun adorning the sky, or like a polished mirror set upon its stand.
Without passing even a single thought, one immediately achieves perfect enlightenment. Not only does one clarify this great matter, but so too did all the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the past.
Having thoroughly penetrated to the very top and the very bottom of all differentiated causes and conditions, the Buddha-dharma and worldly dharmas are forged into a single whole.
One proceeds with effortless spontaneity—spontaneously and effortlessly—free and easy, pure and clean, becoming a peerless true person of the Way who is unconditioned and without affairs.
Only after such an appearance in the world can one say that one has not failed the lifelong pursuit of the Dharma.

This is merely the aspiration of one who studies. If such a thought is slight and the resolve is not fierce and sharp, it will be *wei wei* (feeble), *wang wang* (vague), and *liang liang* (unsubstantial).
Today it is thus; tomorrow it is thus. Even if one applies effort for thirty or twenty years, it will be just like water soaking a stone.
Look at this; when the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives...
"Ten people make five pairs; [if you act with] such meager courtesy and depart, it will cause those who are late learners and beginners not to give rise to reverence and admiration.
As for a fellow like this—if he were to come before the gate of Gao Feng, I would beat him to death ten thousand times over; what crime would that be?"
Today, among my assembly, there are none who are not sharp hawks or swift falcons, like dragons or tigers. With one raised, they clarify three;
their eyes perceive the slightest shift in weight. How could they ever adopt such a manner as this—staring blankly while passing the time?
Even so, at such a moment, what exactly do you call "the one great matter"? If you can say it, I shall grant it to you.
"Thirty blows of the staff! If you cannot say it, I shall likewise give you thirty blows of the staff. Why? (He strikes the staff once and says:
Under the gate of Gao Feng, rewards and punishments are distinct.
I have come here for twenty-four years; I have constantly been in sickness, seeking physicians and taking medicine, having exhausted every possible means."
In his hardship and suffering, he realized that his illness had reached the *gao-huang*—a point where no medicine could heal it.
Later, at Shuangjing, he dreamed of ingesting the elixir bestowed by Master Duqiao. On the sixth day, unexpectedly, the poison lodged within him by the old master of Yangshan was triggered;
his soul fled and his courage failed, and only after death did he return to life. At that moment, he suddenly became aware of the four elements (*catvāri mahābhūtāni*).
Lightness and ease—like setting down a carrying pole weighing one hundred and twenty catties. Now I shall bestow this elixir universally upon the great assembly;

you all should take it. First, take these six sense organs and six consciousnesses, the four elements and five aggregates, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth, and the myriad phenomena of the universe, and melt them all together into a single mass of doubt, suddenly present before you, without requiring even a single stroke of the spear.
A single banner, silent and still, is like a world of peace and tranquility. Even walking like this is merely a mass of doubt;
sitting like this is also a mass of doubt; putting on clothes and eating food is also a mass of doubt;
even defecating and urinating is also a mass of doubt. Extending to seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing—all are entirely nothing but doubt.

The "ball" (tuán): through doubting and doubting again, until doubt reaches the point where effort is exhausted, that is precisely where one gains strength. Without doubting, there is spontaneous doubt;
without lifting it up, it is spontaneously lifted. From morning until evening, it adheres head to tail, forged into a single whole without so much as a hair’s breadth of seam or fissure.
Shaken, it does not move; pursued, it does not depart. Radiant and numinous, it is ever present before one. It is like a boat sailing with the current, requiring no manual effort at all.
This very state is the moment when one gains true mastery. Furthermore, you must make your right mindfulness sincere and be careful not to harbor a dualistic mind.
Polish it further and further, refine it through repeated elimination, until the profound mysteries and ultimate depths are exhausted, reaching the most supreme and ultimate limit.
Subtle! To settle one’s body upon the tip of a single hair—solitary and remote, towering and majestic, unmoving and unshakable, neither coming nor going.
When not a single thought arises, the past and future limits are severed. From this point on, worldly toil is suddenly stilled and dullness and distraction are eradicated.
Walking, one does not know that one walks; sitting, one does not know that one sits; cold, one does not know that it is cold; heat, one does not know that it is hot.
One knows the heat; yet when drinking tea, one does not know it is tea, and when eating rice, one does not know it is rice.
All day long, one remains in a state of dull stupidity, exactly like something carved from clay or wood. Therefore, it is said that one is no different from a wall.
As soon as this state manifests before you, it is the news of having arrived home. You are certainly not far from the ground. You have grasped it; you have seized it.
It is simply a matter of waiting for the right moment. Yet, one must not act as if one is seeing such a thing.
One must not give rise to a thought of diligence to seek it; nor must one use the mind to wait for it.
One must not intend to let go of a single thought, nor must one intend to abandon a single thought. One must simply maintain firm and concentrated right mindfulness, taking awakening as the standard.
At this moment, eighty-four thousand demonic armies are waiting at the gates of your six sense-faculties.

All manner of extraordinary, marvelous, and sublime events—whether auspicious or inauspicious, and whether they manifest as omens or responses—arise according to what your mind conceives, according to what your mind generates, according to what your mind seeks, and according to what your mind manifests.
Whatever you desire shall be fulfilled without exception. If you should even for a moment...
If you give rise to a mind of even the slightest distinction, or conceive a single speck of deluded thought, you will immediately fall into the trap of others;
you will immediately be made their master, and immediately be subject to their commands. Thereupon, you will speak demonic words with your mouth and practice demonic deeds with your mind.
You will instead slander others as being wrong and praise yourself as following the true Way. From this point on, the primary cause of Prajñā will be forever extinguished, and the seed of Bodhi—
The seedling will no longer sprout. Throughout kalpa after kalpa and birth after birth, they shall always be companions.
You should know that all these demonic realms arise from one’s own mind and are produced by one’s own mind; if the mind does not arise, what can be done about them? Tiantai said:
"Your skillful means are finite; my non-appropriation is infinite. Truly, these words are so!
However, simply let everything go until it becomes cold and clear, until it is level and settled, until it is pure and free from even a single speck of defilement.
To go from one thought-moment to ten thousand years is like being a corpse-guarding ghost;
guarding and guarding until this ball of doubt suddenly bursts with a loud crack—take it for granted that it will shake heaven and move earth. Exert yourself! Exert yourself!
To Layman Zhigong (Hong Xin'en):
Throughout the day we have conversed on non-duality, yet I have never uttered a single word. You ask again what this meaning is; we cannot help but leave each other in a state of mutual stagnation.
"One's parents are not one's kin; who is the most intimate? The blind turtle and the lame tortoise—how sharp and alert they are!

Han Xiang previously attained realization within this very realm; he saw that boundless lands and their environments are not separated by so much as a hair’s breadth, and that the ten ages of past and present do not depart from the present moment of thought.
If this is not yet the case for you, it does not matter—simply pivot the wheel of the mechanism.
Then, apply your full attention to the blind turtle and the lame tortoise; give rise to a state of doubt.
By doubting and doubting until it reaches its limit, you must bring the internal and external into a single whole, so that throughout the day there is not even a hair’s breadth of leakage.
Let this remain firmly lodged in your breast like a lethal poison, or like a vajra-ring or a thorny jujube fruit—determined to swallow it, determined to pass through it.
Simply exhaust all the skills and techniques of your entire life and cast them away with indignation; naturally, a place of awakening will arise.

Even if you cannot swallow and penetrate it in this life, at the moment your eyes fall to the ground—regardless of whether you are in the various evil realms—you will be neither startled nor terrified, free from all constraints and fetters.
Should you encounter the Old Man of Yama or the various great ghost kings, they too will fold their hands in submission. Why is this? It is because...
It is because this Prajñā possesses such inconceivable power. Nevertheless, even when there are various karmic actions from the present life, ultimately the power of Prajñā is superior;
it is like a vajra-pillar that cannot be pierced by drilling nor shaken by shaking.
When a person emerges from a family of great influence and power, they are likewise treated thus: none among all the officials, subordinates, or soldiers fail to stand in awe of them.
Furthermore, if one were to cast something onto the ground, it would first land where it is heaviest;

likewise, although there are the appearances of formation, abiding, decay, and emptiness, they are like a dragon shedding its skin or a traveler staying in a lodging—the true master is fundamentally without birth or extinction, without going or coming.

There is no increase and no decrease; there is no aging and no youth. From beginningless kalpas until this present life, though one has emerged and submerged, undergone thousands of transformations and myriad changes, it has never shifted by even a hair’s breadth.

How lamentable that those of us who study the Way often mistake this consciousness-spirit for the truth, failing to rectify their realization and failing to escape birth and death. Setting that aside for now, consider this present life:
Once this seed of Prajñā has been sown, as soon as it emerges, one will surely possess both merit and wisdom, transcending the present and surpassing the past.
Those such as Prime Minister Pei, Prince Li, Han Yu, Bai Juyi, Su Shi, and Zhang Fangping are examples of this.
Although they were deeply immersed in the realms of desire and had never applied effort, as soon as they encountered a true spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), [they attained realization].
Upon a single word, they suddenly awaken to the Supreme Vehicle and transcend birth and death. Though remaining amidst the dust of the world, they sport in samādhi;
never forgetting the Buddha’s entrustment, they protect my gate from without and all carry the ancestral lamp, continuing the life-force of the Buddha's wisdom.
Were these people not nurtured by their past lives, how could they suddenly blossom and bear fruit in such a manner? Thus, they are both fulfilled in merit and fulfilled in wisdom. This is indeed so.
That is indeed so. Today, this mountain monk, however, possesses a medicinal herb that forges the ordinary into the sacred, a seed that requires no planting or nurturing.
To explain it would be prolix; I shall briefly cite a verse: If you wish to understand the cause of the seed, Read "The Great Man Above" thoroughly.
If you reach the point of "knowing the rites," The blind turtle and the lame tortoise will become kin.
In establishing the retreat, the great limit is ninety days and the small limit is seven days. Within the coarse there is the subtle; within the subtle there is the profound.

Profoundly and profoundly, without interval, not even a speck of dust can stand. At this very moment, it is like a silver mountain and an iron wall: advancing, there is no door; retreating, one loses the way.
It is like falling into a pit ten thousand fathoms deep, with precipitous cliffs and thorny brambles on all four sides.

One must absolutely be a fierce hero, determined to turn one’s body and leap out. If there is even a single moment of hesitation, even the Buddha cannot save you. This is the most supreme, profound gate.

If, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, you can truly fulfill these three requirements, you may rest assured that success will be achieved within days; there is no need to fear a turtle escaping from its jar. Should you lack even one of these...
First: It is like a cauldron with a broken leg; it will ultimately become a discarded vessel.
Nevertheless, even though this is so, if it falls into the pit at West Peak, one cannot help but rescue it. *Du!* (A shout of exhortation.)

(He brandishes his staff and says: This one point—though the Buddhas and patriarchs of the past sought it, passing through a thousand demons and ten thousand hardships, ten thousand deaths and a thousand births—it flowed like water toward the east;
it would certainly not stop until it reached the vast ocean. By this one may infer.
This is no small matter. If one wishes to turn iron into gold and share the same realm as the thousand sages, how could those of shallow knowledge and narrow vision possibly deliberate upon it?

One must possess the strength to lift cauldrons and pull mountains, a capacity that encompasses heaven and embraces earth, a mechanism for cutting through nails and severing iron, and the hand that strikes the phoenix and nets the dragon.
If you truly possess such skill and strategy, let this staff assist you in manifesting the pivotal moment.
(He strikes the table once and says: "When one has spirit, add more spirit. (Again he strikes the table once and says:
"Where there is no elegance, there is elegance. If one were a lame tortoise or a blind turtle, they could only leap once or twice; their skill would then be exhausted.
Under the gate of West Peak, there is no use for anything at all. (The Master brandishes his staff and calls to the attendant: "Take this and place it upon Lion Rock;
let it surge eastward and submerge westward as it pleases."
If one discusses this matter, true application of effort is certainly not found in walking, standing, sitting, or lying down;
it is certainly not found in putting on clothes or eating food; it is certainly not found in defecating or urinating;
it is certainly not found in speaking or remaining silent, or in movement and stillness. Since this is so, ultimately where does it reside? Listen! If you can understand it right here—
Once you have found the place of rest, you will see that even before emerging from the mother’s womb, you have already walked on foot; you have already come to see the High Peak;
you have already passed the imperial examination with an empty mind; and you have already become capable of engaging with things and benefiting living beings.

Even if your defilements of ignorance are heavy, such that you do not perceive or know [this], you cannot avoid first being moved by concentration and subsequently being uprooted by wisdom. (Truly...)
[He] let out a long shout and said: "A set of unperforated iron hammers.
To demonstrate the principle, he addressed the Great Man:
"In general, when a student first encounters a master of the true lineage, even after ten or twenty years, [they remain stuck] on this side or that."

Whether participating or studying, whether transmitting or recording, they fill their bellies with leftover soup and rancid rice—evil knowledge and evil perceptions, sharp and full to the brim—just like a stinking jar of fermented dregs.
If one with a sense of smell encounters this, they cannot help but feel revulsion and vomit.
Reaching such a state, even if one wishes to recognize one's error and repent, it is already too late. One must establish a new life.
To the very limit. You must empty it out three or four times and wash it seven or eight times.
Wash away the froth until it is perfectly clean and dry, so that not a trace of scent remains. Only then is the elixir of Prajñā fit for pursuit.
If you are negligent and careless, discarding it without making it truly dry, then even if you pour in the finest *amṛta*, it will inevitably turn into a jar of foul poison.
Water. Now tell me, where does the benefit and harm lie? *Pfft!* The toxic vapors have penetrated deep.
To the assembly:
when a skilled physician treats an illness, he first investigates its root. Once the root is found, there is no ailment that cannot be cured. You monks! Complete [your practice].
To have practiced with sincere faith and maintained single-mindedness for ten or twenty years yet remain ignorant of birth and death is because one has failed to investigate their root.

One must know that the notions of self and other are the very root of birth and death, while birth and death are but the leaves of self and other. If one wishes to remove the leaves, one must first address the root.
One must first eliminate the root. Once the root is eliminated, how can its leaves remain?

Nevertheless, even though this is so, how do we know that this root has been planted and nurtured deeply and firmly since time immemorial? Unless one possesses the strength to lift a tripod and pull up a mountain, it will be difficult to eradicate it entirely.
We cannot avoid borrowing the majestic power of this staff to specifically clear away the fever for all of you. (He strikes the ground with the staff.)
(Strike once. Shout once and say: "To toil without merit—if one were to discuss this matter, it requires genuine application of effort.
It is just like a person condemned to death in prison who suddenly encounters a jailer who has become intoxicated and fallen asleep;
he breaks his shackles and chains and flees all night long. Although there are many venomous dragons and fierce tigers along the way,"
Press straight ahead; be utterly without fear. Why? It is simply because of this one word, "urgency" (*qiè*).

If, at the moment of applying effort, you can truly possess such a heart of urgency, you may take it for granted that you will hit the mark a hundred times out of a hundred. Do you have such a hit right now?
(Striking the meditation seat once with the whisk, he says: A hair’s breadth of difference, and heaven and earth stand apart.
(He raises his staff and says: "At this point, both person and dharma are forgotten; the paths of mind and consciousness are cut off. To take a single step is for the great ocean to surge with waves;
to snap one's fingers is for Mount Sumeru to tremble. A lump of clay or a clod of earth emits a great radiance;
a gourd or a winter melon speaks incessantly and ever-blazingly. Even so, if you come before the gate of Xifeng, you cannot avoid having sleeves too short for long arms."

A single peg is briefly revealed; you must directly pierce through the eye of the true gate at the crown of the head and see that the self prior to the empty kalpa and this present illusory physical body are non-dual and without distinction. But tell me, what is the self prior to the empty kalpa?
(He strikes the meditation staff once and says: "The Vajra-eater is struck with an iron staff; the clay ox’s eyes bleed."
Upon concluding the retreat, he addressed the assembly:
"If we discuss this matter, there is neither noble nor base, neither old nor young, neither male nor female, and neither sharp nor dull.
Therefore, on the eighth night of the twelfth month before Mount Bodhi, our World-Honored One beheld the morning star and awakened to the Way, whereupon he said:"
"How marvelous! Sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata. It is further said:
"The mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction. And again: "This Dharma is equal; there is no high or low.

Since there is neither distinction nor high or low, from the Buddhas and Patriarchs of old, through the masters of past and present, down to the elder monks of the world, there has been realization...
Realization may be slow or swift, difficult or easy. Ultimately, how is it so? It is like people here, each with their own household affairs;
suddenly one day, they turn the light back upon themselves and reflect on returning to the source.
Some arrive after a year has passed, some after a month, some after a day, and some...
Some arrive in an instant, while others do not arrive even until death. This is because there are differences in the distance from leaving home;
thus, there are distinctions in the speed, ease, or difficulty of arrival. Nevertheless, in the midst of this, there is a man.
There is no family estate to which one may return; there is no path of meditation to be studied; there is no birth-and-death to be escaped; there is no nirvana to be realized.
All day long, one proceeds freely and spontaneously; proceeding freely and spontaneously. If you can examine this and grasp it, then Śākyamuni and Maitreya—[are but dust upon the ground].
To carry your water jar and hold your alms bowl for you would not be considered an extraordinary favor.
But if it were otherwise—(striking the meditation seat twice with the whisk and shouting twice)—if you go to various places, take care not to misrepresent this.
Addressing the assembly:

If we discuss this extraordinary matter, it is inherently possessed by every person and perfectly realized by each individual. It is like clenching a fist or opening a palm—it does not require the application of even a hair’s breadth of effort.
It is only because the monkey of the mind is restless and the horse of the will is clamorous that one allows oneself to be distracted.

Even if the three poisons and ignorance run rampant, and one falsely clings to the marks of a person, a self, and so forth—like water poured upon ice, making it increasingly thick and solid—it will obstruct one's own numinous light, such that there is certainly no way for it to manifest. This is true unless one is a man forged from raw iron.
This reality must be clearly understood; it is not a matter for haste. You must directly resolve to cultivate great aspiration and establish great vows.

Slay the mind-monkey and the horse of the will; sever delusive thoughts and worldly toil. Be like one mooring a boat at a rapid on a swift current, disregarding danger and ruin, gain and loss, self and others, right and wrong.
Forget sleep and forget food; cut off all thinking and all deliberation, three times by day and three times by night.
Mind following mind in succession, thought following thought in continuity: fix your footing, clench your teeth, hold fast to the rope’s end, and allow not even a hair’s breadth of wavering.
Even if someone were to take your head or sever your hands and feet.
"To gouge out your heart and liver, even unto the end of your life, you truly must not let them go. Only when you reach this point will there be even a slight flavor of genuine practice.
Alas! In this Dharma-ending age, the time since the Sage has long passed; there are many of a superficial sort."
In the end, you do not believe there is a gate of awakening; you merely engage in intellectual excavation here and calculation there.
Even if you were to calculate it to completion and excavate it to perfection, when the light of your eyes falls to the ground [at the moment of death], will it still be of any use?
If it were of any use, then why did the World-Honored One spend six years in the Snowy Mountains, Bodhidharma nine years at Shaolin, and Changqing break seven meditation cushions?
The meditation cushion. It took Xianglin forty years to finally achieve a state of unified focus. Zhaozhou did not allow his mind to be distracted for thirty years;
why must one seek so much and undergo such suffering? Furthermore, there is a certain class of people who work at their practice for ten or twenty years yet never find an entrance;
this is simply because they lack the spiritual bone from past lives and their resolve is not firm.

Half-believing and half-doubting, sometimes rising and sometimes falling, they play with it again and again. As worldly sentiments grow ever more refined, their aspiration for the Way gradually becomes lax.
Throughout the twelve periods of the day, it is difficult to find even a single moment when one can maintain firm control and integrate everything into a single whole.
For those in such a state, even if they were to continue playing until Maitreya’s descent, what connection would there be?
If one is a true, authentic practitioner and a high-minded traveler who refuses to act recklessly, they will, from the very outset, seek out a master of the Way.
Upon hearing even a single word or half-sentence, they do not hesitate;
they immediately believe it as it is, take charge of themselves, and maintain their composure. Thus, they stand solitary and towering, pure and naked, stark and clear.
Do not inquire further of peril and ruin, gain and loss; simply gaze thus. Suddenly, the rope snaps and one is swallowed up;
only after death does one revive again. Behold the natural radiance of the original ground—where else could one seek a Buddha? Furthermore, there is a verse to present to the assembly:
A small boat moored at a rapid rapids— One must firmly grasp that rope-end. Suddenly, the rope...
It is difficult to avoid being cut off; one must simply allow blood to gush from the entire body.
When the myriad dharmas return to the One, to what does that One return? It is only valued when one remains alert and focused on the doubt.
When the doubt reaches the point where emotion is forgotten and the mind is severed, the golden bird flies through the heavens at midnight.
If you exhaustively investigate this matter until the ultimate limit of your effort, it is just like planting flowers in the air or reaching for the moon in water;
there is truly no place for you to apply your hand, and no place for you to direct your mind. Often, as soon as such a state manifests before you, five out of ten people beat the retreat drum.
Little do they realize that this is precisely the news of having arrived home. If one is [like] Meng...
Eighth, O Han, when you reach the point where you cannot bring your hand down and the time for your mind to apply itself has passed, it is like Guan Yu amidst a million-strong army:
disregarding gain or loss, he went straight for Yan Liang.

If you truly possess such strategic skill and such fierce intensity, you can be certain that you will achieve merit in a mere snap of the fingers and become a sage in an instant. If it is not so, even if you practice until you reach Maitreya...
Le was born as a human; he too was merely Master Zhang.
The thirtieth day of the twelfth month—the time of reckoning—is drawing near. Let not the pillar and the lantern fall into further slumber.
Meeting face-to-face, the opportunity is seized; seizing the opportunity, one gazes face-to-face. Suddenly, the eyes are struck blind.
Be careful not to step on a thorn in the soft mud.
New Year’s Eve Small Sermon.
The matter of birth and death is of great importance. Impermanence is swift. Not knowing the place from which one comes when born is called the "greatness of birth.

Not knowing the place to which one goes when dying is called the "greatness of death. This single great matter of birth and death is precisely the vital gateway for practicing Zen and studying the Way;
it is the governing authority for becoming a Buddha or an Ancestor. All Tathāgatas of the three periods and the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, through their myriad transformations—
The manifestation [of Buddhas] appearing in the world is, in truth, the fundamental source of this one great matter of birth and death.

From the four groups of seven patriarchs in the Western Heavens to the two groups of three in the land of Tang, and even down to the elder monks throughout the realm—whether they appeared or vanished, expanded or contracted, acted in reverse or followed the flow to transform others—all were likewise the fundamental source of this one great matter.
Thus, the monastics of Chan from all quarters do not shrink from toil and hardship for thirty years, nor for two...
For ten years, you have been "pushing through the grass to observe the wind" and "rubbing your trousers against the grindstone"; this, too, is the fundamental source of this one great matter.

All of you who have resolved to leave the household life, resolved to travel on pilgrimage, and resolved to come and see Gao Feng—throughout the three watches of the day and the three watches of the night, with brows knitted in concentration—this, too, is the fundamental source of this one great matter.
Across the four modes of birth and the six realms of existence for a thousand kalpas...
For ten thousand kalpas, they change their heads and faces, enduring suffering and bitterness; this too is being deluded regarding the fundamental source of this great matter.
Our Buddha, the World-Honored One, relinquished his position as a Golden Wheel-turning King and practiced austerities for six years in the Snowy Mountains;
seeing the morning star at midnight, he awakened to the Way—this too is awakening to the fundamental source of this great matter. Master Bodhidharma came to this land.
Sengcan faced the wall at Shaolin for nine years; Huikong severed his arm.

At the very place where the mind cannot be found, they lost their nostrils—this too is the fundamental source of the great matter for those who have attained awakening. Linji suffered sixty bitter blows from Huangbo.
Returning the fist to the ribs of Dayu was also the very source of the great matter of the awakened ones.

Lingyun’s peach blossoms, Xiangyan’s striking the bamboo, Changqing’s rolling up the curtain, and Xuansha’s pointing at his finger—even down to all the masters of antiquity who attained realization and verification, benefiting sentient beings and guiding others, none of them ever transcended the very source of the great matter of the awakened ones. This is often seen...

Fellow practitioners of the Way: although you are said to have entered this single gate, you often fail to understand the fundamental source of studying the Path and cannot rouse your resolve, merely passing your days in negligence.
Now, to avoid further entanglements, I shall cite the causes by which the Buddhas and Patriarchs entered the Way and the means by which they attained realization as a standard of excellence.
Only then will those of late learning and initial capacity be able to direct themselves toward it. Furthermore—
How does one proceed on the Way? An ancient did not say: "If you wish to be liberated from birth and death, you must pass through the Patriarch’s barrier.
Ultimately, what constitutes this barrier? To call it a "bamboo stick" is to encounter resistance; not to call it a "bamboo stick" is to turn one's back.

There must not be speech; there must not be silence. If you can fix a single eye upon this very point and see through it, you will turn your body, penetrate the vital breath, and pass through without obstruction.
There will be no dharma that is not understood. Every headland manifests, and every object is fully revealed.
Boundless lands and realms—self and other—are not separated by so much as a hair’s tip. Ten ages of past and present—their beginning and end—are not distinct.
Free from present thought. Thus, when the Master Shaolun (Water-Lake) saw the Great Master Mazu, he prostrated himself;
as he rose to pose a question, Mazu seized him by the chest and kicked him down.

As he got up, Mazu laughed heartily and said, "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates and immeasurable subtle meanings—recognize their source entirely upon the tip of a single hair. Deshan saw Longtan...
At the spot where the wind had nearly extinguished the paper candle, Tan was suddenly and completely enlightened.
The following day, he took his commentaries and treatises to the Dharma Hall and burned them, saying: "To exhaust all profound dialectics is like placing a single hair in the great void;
to exhaust all worldly mechanisms is like casting a single drop into a vast abyss. Reaching this point, what Chan or Way is there to investigate? What Buddha-dharma is there?"
One may study thus: what birth-and-death is there to be liberated from? What nirvāṇa is there to be realized? One proceeds freely and spontaneously;
one is free and spontaneous in proceeding. When the thirtieth day of the twelfth month arrives, one will surely attain great mastery, moving and abiding with complete autonomy.
Thus it is said: "Since recognizing the path of Caoxi, I have known that birth-and-death are not mutually concerned. Although it is so...
"It is so. (He brandishes the whisk and says: "Now tell me, is this life or is it death?
If you can speak thus, you may immediately claim supremacy where there is no Buddha and preach the Dharma where there is no Dharma.

If you have not yet reached this realization, I, this mountain monk, shall not fear shame, but will further reveal a message to all of you. (With the whisk, he makes a gesture of fishing and says: "The night is cold."
The fish hides in the depths while one casts the hook below; it is better to gather it in and pass the remainder of the year.
Again, it is said: At Beichan, at the end of the year, they cook the white ox of the open field, and all manner of rare delicacies are fully provided.
At Fenggao, at the end of the year, although there are a hundred holes and a thousand sores, he insists on taking the non-existent and making it existent, finely slicing the clouds atop the peaks.
Thinly sliced is the moon at the bottom of the lake; freshly prepared, it is piled high in an extraordinary arrangement.

This is intended so that everyone’s bowels shall be full and their bellies stuffed, and that every person may forever be free from hunger and emptiness. But tell me: is this the same as the ancients, or is it different?
Those who possess eyes and have tongues, try to discern it!
Addressing the assembly:

If we discuss attaining realization by fixing a specific deadline, it is like a person carrying snow to fill a well—undaunted by cold or heat, making no distinction between day and night, carrying it horizontally and carrying it vertically, carrying it whether it is right or wrong.
Carrying it back and forth, even if one continues for years...

Passing through years, even unto ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, throughout that interval, one attains conviction, treads with stability, maintains steadfastness, and acts as the master;

never for a single thought arises a mind of weary detachment, never for a single thought arises a mind of indolence, never for a single thought arises a mind of doubt, and never for a single thought arises a mind seeking fulfillment. If one can truly reach such a state, then indeed—
If one possesses such an air of magnanimity, upon reaching this point, one may be certain that both person and dharma are forgotten, and mind and consciousness are both extinguished.
One’s form is like withered wood or a rotten stump; one’s will is like that of an infant or a young child. Suddenly, the burden is abruptly severed and shattered. Yongjia said:
"The myriad worlds of the great chiliocosm are bubbles in the sea; all sages and worthies are like lightning strikes. This is truly excellent.

Thirty more blows of the staff. If you say that this matter has been investigated, awakened to, explained, practiced, come to, and gone from—though it may be so—you must still wait for another thirty years before you have attained it. Why?
Because while the two horns and four hooves have all passed through, the tail has not yet cleared.
If one discusses this matter, it is like throwing a single stone into a ten-thousand-fathom deep pool:

it penetrates to the very top and the very bottom, without the slightest interval remaining. If one can truly apply effort in this manner and maintain such continuity for seven days, [the realization will occur].
If one errs in severing [delusions], (So-and-so) shall fall forever into the Avīci Hell.
Having bound the assembly and signaled them,
he caps the head of his staff, ties the mouth of his cloth bag, imprisons himself within the Iron Ring Mountains, and adds heavy shackles upon his neck.
From within existence, one extracts non-existence; from within non-existence, one extracts existence. There are hundreds of thousands of kinds of agony, yet one does not escape this old trap.
Great assembly, tell me: what do you call this "trap"? Even if you can discern it clearly, you must still see Xifeng.
"Beyond that, even further beyond. This one point of being for oneself and not for others—wait until thirty years from now.
[He addresses the assembly, holding up his staff and calling out: "Do you see? Everyone has eyes in their heads; you are not blind men."
"It is certainly seeing. (He strikes once with his staff and says: "Do you hear? Every single one of you has blood under your skin;
you are not dead men. It is certainly hearing. Since it is both seen and heard, what is it? (He draws a circle with his staff.)

Let us set aside seeing and hearing for a moment. Consider this: before the six sense organs were fully formed, and before sounds and forms had manifested—this "hearing of what has not been heard" and "seeing of what has not been seen. At such a time, by what means can one verify it?
(He strikes with the staff. [Symbol: ○@│] I now guarantee this matter for you; it shall never be in vain. (He strikes with the staff. [Symbol: ○@□] Thirty years.
Afterwards, you must by all means refrain from falsely communicating news [of your progress] (he leans on his staff and descends from the seat).
As for this matter, it requires only that one have a sense of urgency within oneself. Once there is a sense of urgency, genuine doubt will arise.
When true doubt arises, one does not belong to the gradual stages; rather, one is able to immediately bring the afflictions to rest and eliminate dullness and distraction.

When not a single thought arises and the boundaries of past and future are severed—once you reach such a moment, you may be certain that the door will push open and you will fall right into the mortar.
If this mindfulness is not urgent, true doubt will not arise; even if you wear out a million or ten million bundles of *pútuán* grass, it will still be like striking the third watch at midday.
Within delusion there is awakening; awakening returns once more to delusion. One must simply forget both delusion and awakening, and cast aside both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*).

Only then, within the gate of the patch-robed monks, is there a basis for conversation. "Great assembly, since delusion and awakening have both been forgotten and person and phenomena have both been cast aside, who then is it that converses with you? Speak quickly! Speak quickly!"
If one discusses this matter, it is like ascending a high mountain ten thousand *ren* tall. Step by step, one draws near to the summit;

yet there remain only a few steps where the cliff is sheer and climbing is impossible. Reaching this point, one must be a person forged from pure steel, prepared to sacrifice life and body, gazing left and right, looking and looking again, making the ultimate as the goal.
Even if it takes a thousand lifetimes or ten thousand kalpas—ten thousand... [the path remains].
Though he faced a thousand demons, this mind and this resolve became ever firmer and ever stronger.
If the root were not real, how could those who are merely superficial even hope to approach the precipice? They would surely retreat upon hearing the wind of his fame.
A Small Sermon for the Eve of the New Year: Of the three hundred and sixty days of a year, look, look—this very night has come to its end.

Out of ten people, five or six have been practicing Zen, yet they do not know Zen; they have been studying the Way, yet they do not recognize the Way. These four characters—“not knowing” and “not recognizing”—are precisely [the point].
This is the marrow and bone of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; it is the root source of the entire Great Canon.

A person of keen faculties, upon merely hearing it mentioned, is like a dragon obtaining water or a tiger relying on its mountain; they move with unimpeded mastery throughout heaven and earth. And yet, even though this is so—
If you examine this closely, it is still just news from "this side. If you claim it is a single move from "that side" or even further beyond that, then let me tell you:
even the Seven Patriarchs of the Western Heaven, the Two or Three Masters of the Tang land, and all the ancient sages throughout the world—dare I say they have not yet reached the ultimate.
When I, this mountain monk, announce it in this way, there may suddenly be a man whose heart is indignant and whose mouth is hesitant to speak.
He came out and said, "Gao Feng! Gao Feng! What longings do you have that you can open such a large mouth?
To which he simply replied: "Next year there will be new branches; the spring breeze shall not cease its turmoil."
I address the assembly:
all day long I wear clothes, yet never so much as a single thread is attached; all day long I eat rice, yet never so much as a single grain is chewed.
Since this is so, tell me: what is it that you are wearing on your body right now, and what is it that you are eating with your mouth every day?

What is this? Arriving at this point, regardless of whether one is enlightened or unenlightened, thorough or not thorough, even a single thread or a drop of water must be repaid by pulling the plow and dragging the harrow for him.
Why? A single mass of white clouds spans the mouth of the valley;
how many returning birds lose their way to their nests?
If we discuss this matter, it is just like cornering a dog against a wall.
No matter how much one corners it, until it is driven into a sharp corner, it cannot help but turn around and take a bite. Is there anyone here now who has been bitten?
(He strikes the meditation staff once and says: "Alas! Alas!"
Study the Way as you did at the beginning, never changing your mind; through a thousand demons and ten thousand hardships, become ever more alert.
You must strike out the marrow of empty space and pull out the nail behind the diamond-hard head.
If we discuss this matter, at the time of applying effort, it is just like forging an iron boat to enter the sea to retrieve the wish-fulfilling jewel.
Do not concern yourself with whether you can forge it or not; simply let Meng Bala forge on.
Suddenly, one day, when the forging is complete, he has entered the sea and obtained the jewel. When he brings it here to present to this old monk, I cannot help but give him one [blow].
"Strike and shatter it! Why? Have you not seen it said: 'Existence is used for profit; non-existence is used for function'?
If we speak of true participation and true awakening, it is just like an eighty-year-old man pulling a bottomless iron boat against the wind and the current.
It matters not whether he goes up or does not go up, whether he penetrates or does not penetrate; one must simply [apply] the mind."
The mind is without interval; from moment to moment, there is no deficiency. Step by step, one exhausts all the skillful means of a lifetime to gaze forward.
When one reaches the place where the feet can find no footing, and the sinews snap and the bones break, suddenly the waters turn and the winds reverse—this is the news of arriving home.
Is there anyone here now who has arrived home? (He strikes the meditation staff once and says: "One hundred and eight thousand miles."
A thousand [times].

If one discusses this matter, it does not require long kalpas of cultivation, nor the accumulation of merit and virtue; it makes no distinction between the worthy and the foolish, the sharp and the dull, nor between those of long practice and beginners.
It values only the "Man of Eight" (Mèng Bāláng Hàn) who, regardless of peril or loss, gives rise to great indignation.
Resolve: arouse a great state of doubt, like the youth Sudhana when he visited the Brahmin Śīghra-uṣṇa and cast himself into a mass of blazing fire.
At such a moment, both person and dharma are forgotten, and the workings of the mind are extinguished.
Whether you turn left or right, wherever you stumble or strike, it is either Dongshan’s "three pounds of flax" or Yunmen’s "dry dung pellet. If you can still [hesitate]...
Tàn wèi, tàn cuī, tàn cuī. Wǎng wǎng liǎng liǎng. Do not say you have personally seen Gao Feng;
even if you were to go through the belly of the Old Barbarian, you would still be left with nothing at all.
In response to the letter from Layman Zhizhong:
The questions set forth in your correspondence all concern the points of doubt regarding the diligent practice of students;
I shall resolve them so that those of late learning and initial capacity may proceed toward the Way without obstruction. You ask: "Is the ordinary mind the Way? Is the mindless state the Way? This—
The saying that "ordinary mind is no-mind" has brought fulfillment to so many, yet it has also led so many astray.

Often, people fail to realize there are thorns within the mud and knives within the smile. How much more so than those who "brandish a staff to strike at the moon" or "join bamboo poles to point toward the heavens"?
When the ancients offered a single word or half a phrase, it was like brandishing a sharp, polished blade, intending from the very start to sever the person.
The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). If you are one who has blood beneath your skin, you will directly take it up without further deliberation.
